svg.text: Taxonomy has two golden ages and two world wars in it.
anyone asking which marine groups are still being described
whether a class's taxonomy is finished or still open
the recent rise is names being revised rather than species
marine species described, all nineteen classes pooled
peak 2005–09, the larger of the two
1915–19 sits 30% below what its neighbours imply and 1945–49 sits 31% below.
Description is done by a few hundred specialists in a handful of
institutions, and both wars closed them. The recovery overshoots: more
marine species were described in the 2000s than in any decade of the age of
and which taxonomies are still open
each curve scaled to its own peak; ordered by the rate on the right
number is new species per year per 1,000 already known, measured between the two rules
Bristle worms gain 11.9 species a year per thousand they already have and
seabirds gain none at all. Sharks and rays are the surprise at 8.2, as open
as the worms and sponges despite being large, conspicuous and only 1,164
species — so being noticed is not the same as being described. The raw count
of new species would have ranked crabs first and said nothing: it tracks
OBIS v3 checklist, fetched 2026-09-18, year parsed from scientificNameAuthorship — the FIRST year in the string, which is the original description, so
"(Pallas, 1766)" is 1766. Only taxonRank Species rows are counted, because a checklist also carries genera and the class itself with their own
authorships. The checklist caps at 10,000 rows, 500s above that, and is sorted by record count descending, so it is paged with skip — from, offset and
after are accepted and silently ignored. Page one alone would have given a gastropod median of 1864 against 1911, and a crab median of 1903 against
1966. Bins run to 2024: the 2025–29 bin is one year old and is dropped rather than drawn as a fall.
